items.question: How do you view the emphasis on math benchmarks when your goal is to train a model that's great at everything?
items.object: Math-focused benchmarks for training general-purpose AI models
items.answer: Well, yeah. I mean, in general, I'm all for generality. Let's train something that's great at everything. It is important. I was skeptical at first of this intense focus on things like math, but it is very important to have good benchmarks that are going to encourage you to be able to reason about difficult tasks, because a lot of things will drop perplexity, like add more parameters to the model.
quotes: Well, yeah. I mean, in general, I'm all for generality. Let's train something that's great at everything. It is important. I was skeptical at first of this intense focus on things like math, but it is very important to have good benchmarks that are going to encourage you to be able to reason about difficult tasks, because a lot of things will drop perplexity, like add more parameters to the model.

rubrics.text: The response identifies encouraging reasoning about difficult tasks as a justification for emphasizing math benchmarks.

items.question: Why do you see AI helping build its successor as such an important milestone?
items.object: Reinforcement loops in AI development
items.answer: I'd say when Gemini 3.0 writes Gemini 4.0—or I should say Gemini X writes Gemini X plus one. I think these reinforcement loops are probably the most important thing to pay attention to. There are several reinforcement loops going on. The one I just mentioned is probably the most important one: that we can actually use the AI we're building as a tool to make ourselves more productive at building AI. But then there are other reinforcement loops around data flywheels. You have people use these models and provide feedback and make them better at the things that people care about. I think we'll see huge acceleration from that. And then there's just the global excitement and funding flywheel, which also seems to be kicking up in the last few years.

items.question: Why do you think it made sense for AI models to start with text rather than images?
items.object: Text versus images as a starting point for AI models
items.answer: I think it made sense to start with text. A picture is worth a thousand words, but it's a million pixels, so text is still a thousand times more information-dense, just to do math on cliches. There's also a lot more in the main training data for text. We have so many examples of text, which represents the way humans receive and produce information through language, but we have a lot fewer examples—where for something like image generation, you don't have examples of people generating images, so things are a little more challenging. But, as Jack said, great stuff happening.
quotes: It made sense to start with text. A picture is worth a thousand words, but it's a million pixels, so text is still a thousand times more information-dense, just to do math on cliches.

The response identifies the lack of examples of humans producing images as a training-data disadvantage of image generation relative to text generation.

items.question: How do you think AI agents need to improve to handle the complexity and reliability demands of widespread use?
items.object: General solutions for AI agent control and reliability
items.answer: I mean, one is just make the model smarter. That will always help. Most likely, you need very general solutions for these control problems, just like you need general solutions for the intelligence problems, because people are going to use these things in so many unforeseen ways. You can't anticipate it. The users are smarter than the developers in figuring out the use cases. No one envisioned, when they invented the internet, what the internet was going to be for.

items.object: Ilya's view that advancing AI requires an entirely new direction
items.answer: Yes, I pretty much agree, because LLM search is too cheap. Operations cost under 10 to the negative $18 these days.

items.question: How do you assess the potential for making AI systems smarter by spending more compute at inference time?
items.object: Scaling AI capabilities through inference-time compute
items.answer: A million tokens per dollar. You can just check the prices on Gemini. That's orders of magnitude below the cost of most other things you can think of. If you think of a really cheap pastime, like go buy a paperback book and read it, you're paying like 10,000 tokens per dollar. We're a couple of orders of magnitude cheaper than reading a book, probably four orders of magnitude cheaper than paying anybody to do anything, and six, eight orders of magnitude cheaper than paying a software engineer. There's a huge margin of difference there to apply more compute and make the thing smarter. If the value is there, which I think it is, would you pay five cents an hour for the bad engineer or ten cents an hour for the good engineer? There's a huge amount of unexploited flops in there to use if we can find ways to use them. One way straightforwardly is just train a bigger, better model. We're already doing that, but model training costs tend to go up quadratically with the size of the models, and you still end up with relatively cheap inference if we do it right. So then, of course, what everyone is doing now is just applying more compute at inference time through this chain-of-thought thinking or any other brilliant algorithms we can come up with. I think we're just going to start seeing a scaling curve there as well as we're seeing in a lot of places. But does that scale us all the way to the AGI future people envision?

items.question: Why do you see mathematical discovery as a promising test of whether AI can go beyond imitating people?
items.object: Mathematical discovery as a test of whether AI can go beyond imitating people
items.answer: Math is a great example because it's a field where you don't actually need more data. People invented all this math without external input, a lot of times in a room just thinking. You just go into a room, and there are examples where there's some data, like Isaac Newton takes a bunch of astronomical observations, goes into quarantine in his house, and then in physics or something. That's an example where there's data, but nobody actually knows physics, and then you generate physics. Math is even crazier because you start with roughly no data and invent something useful. I think that could provide a counterproof to the assertion that this is just learning to mimic people, that the most we can do with AI is relearn what everybody knows.
quotes: Math is a great example because it's a field where you don't actually need more data. People invented all this math without external input, a lot of times in a room just thinking.

rubrics.text: The response states that mathematical discovery can produce useful knowledge from roughly no external data.
The response argues that AI making novel mathematical discoveries could refute the claim that AI can only relearn existing human knowledge.

items.question: How do you view the debate over whether AI can generate completely novel ideas?
items.object: The debate over whether AI can generate completely novel ideas
items.answer: I don't know. I guess I'd just throw it back at Yann LeCun to prove that he generated a completely novel idea. We'll see. I don't actually care about arguing this stuff. Let's just build AI, greatly increase the level of technology in the world, help people. That seems good enough for me.

items.question: How do you think about the role of experimentation in understanding why AI methods work?
items.object: Experimentation in AI research
items.answer: I think maybe AI research is kind of where chemistry was in the 15th century. It's more alchemy. We don't know why it works. It's highly experimental. You get some idea, but the proof is always in trying it out, and then you have various observations and come to a hypothesis about why this thing works, what's the key thing. Sometimes you're right, sometimes you're wrong. It usually takes more experimentation to find out. Or you can just claim it works because of my magic XYZ, and you have your assistant swallowing frogs or something, or the equivalent.

items.question: How do you think credit should be assigned in collaborative AI research?
items.object: Credit assignment and collaboration in AI research
items.answer: I find naturally researchers love to share and get excited about what they're doing. It is always important to try to credit people liberally because it's often very complicated to tell what idea led to what idea, what was the key insight. At some point we'll have to give up on credit assignment temporarily and take a superintelligence-based approach: we'll wait for the superintelligence to sort it all out, get credit for once we get it. Superintelligence will write some great thought pieces on the culture that drove these transformations. It is super fun working at Google with this group of brilliant people and collaborating with everybody.

items.question: How do you think AI research would have progressed if the chance encounter behind the Transformer hadn't happened?
items.object: The role of chance in the invention of the Transformer
items.answer: We would have all been using LSTMs or something. I mean, I guess maybe it's like if somebody hadn't invented an internal combustion engine, would we still be using steam engines at this point? I think someone would have come up with something.
quotes: We would have all been using LSTMs or something. I mean, I guess maybe it's like if somebody hadn't invented an internal combustion engine, would we still be using steam engines at this point? I think someone would have come up with something.

rubrics.text: The response suggests that someone would likely have developed an alternative to LSTMs even without the chance encounter that led to the Transformer.

items.question: How do you think about the trade-offs between bottom-up and top-down compute allocation in AI research?
items.object: Bottom-up versus top-down compute allocation in AI research
items.answer: We've been through both, or I've been through both. Google Brain previously was mostly bottom-up, as you describe, and DeepMind has been mostly top-down. Different philosophies, and there are pluses and minuses to both. Top-down can be good for getting people to collaborate and getting larger training runs working. Bottom-up is also great for collaboration because you bring someone new on your project; it doesn't mean you have fewer resources per person, you have more total resources. There are so many abstraction-breaking ideas that there's no great way to categorize them. If you're saying this is the compute for pretraining and this is the compute for post-training, you've got something completely different that doesn't fall into those things nicely, and then it falls between the cracks. We are bringing back a good measure of bottoms-up because I think that's super important.

items.question: Why do you think a high-value application like an AI doctor probably doesn't need a task-specific model?
items.object: Task-specific AI models for healthcare
items.answer: I probably don't really think you would need very specific, task-specific models for something that high-value, because you probably pay like a dollar a token for talking to your doctors. The LLM is way, way, way cheaper at this point. So the only reason for task-specific models is price. If there are things you wouldn't pay a dollar a token for, something to analyze vast quantities of data for marginal value, then maybe you want something more targeted.

items.question: How do you decide whether capabilities should share one general model or be split into specialized models?
items.object: Transfer between tasks as a criterion for model specialization
items.answer: There's always this notion there'll be tons of negative transfer out there, so compartmentalize things. I don't really feel like that has ended up being the case. If it could be measured, then that's a good reason to compartmentalize models. If there's no negative transfer, there's positive transfer, then just have one big model. That's my personal philosophy. This isn't something people have uniform agreement over, though; it's an active area of research, how much you want to specialize and spin off these expert models. From the way I see it, it's very simple: if there's positive transfer, put it in the same model as long as it doesn't become too expensive to serve.

items.question: How do you think about the amount of compute needed to make AI breakthroughs today?
items.object: Compute requirements for AI breakthroughs
items.answer: The amount of compute out there—now a kid in the garage has more compute than was necessary to invent the Transformer. People always worry, “Oh, just how much compute do they have?” I think it is definitely possible to make breakthroughs with way less compute than you would imagine.

items.object: The gap between closed-source and open-source AI models
items.answer: It seems like the time gap between closed-source and open-source has been shrinking. I think the technology will continue to accelerate, so it could be that the quality gap will be large and the time gap will be very small. We'll have to see how it plays out. It's super exciting to see all these companies getting great results.

items.question: How do you think the prospect of AI changing humanity's future affects what is worth doing now?
items.object: Meaningful action in a future shaped by AI
items.answer: It's extremely hard to predict what the future will be like. We'll all do our best to make sure AI will be safe and beneficial. It does make you think that what I do now really matters. We don't know if human labor will be materially necessary in the future, but that just means it makes more difference. If you want to do something that matters materially, go do it now. Other than that, try to be a good person. Whatever you find spiritually meaningful, go do it, because maybe that's the purpose of humanity in the future. It may not be about providing for physical needs. We've got to figure out where we find meaning in the future, but we'll have plenty of time for—

items.question: How do you think the need to avoid starvation shaped people's sense of meaning in work in the distant past?
items.object: Meaning in work when survival depends on it
items.answer: We have less meaning than in the past in the sense that in the distant past everyone was at the brink of starvation. “I have meaning in my work because I have to work hard today and get some money so my family doesn't starve tomorrow.”

items.question: What did you think the LLM industry most needed when you left Google to start Character?
items.object: Character as a way for people to discover uses for LLMs
items.answer: The main reason I left Google to start Character was I thought the biggest thing the LLM industry could use was an application where anybody can go and interact with LLMs and discover use cases that were good for them. This was before ChatGPT launched, before Gemini launched. Mission accomplished: everyone's out there talking to LLMs now.

items.question: How did you think about what kind of product Character should become?
items.object: Character's open-ended product approach and entertainment uses
items.answer: Going into Character, we were not really focused on, “Hey, this is going to be an entertainment product or something else.” We went in with an open mind and said, “We're going to put this out there in a general way. We're going to help people conceptualize this as, this thing can take on different personas,” meaning it's a very general technology. See what you can make it do. We found a lot of people are using it for entertainment, partially because at that point in the technology nobody had figured out how to make this thing not hallucinate, so people use it for applications where hallucination is actually a feature, such as entertainment. I think that's worked pretty well. I know a lot of people like using Character.

items.question: How do you see the future of people interacting with AI that feels human?
items.object: The future of humanlike AI interactions
items.answer: I do not know. I think people will always want relationships with humans because it's spiritually more meaningful. But people will like having AIs that are more in human form for things they want. Imagine you just got elected president and you get your piece in the cabinet to advise you wherever you go. You get your own personal AI cabinet, a good AI summarization of all the secrets. Or maybe you're CEO of your own AI company so you get a lot more productivity. In a lot of those cases it's less about the personality and more about the productivity. But to the degree that people like interacting with something that feels human, probably we'll see a lot of AI that feels more human in various ways.

items.question: What do you see as the infrastructure challenge for Transformer inference compared with training?
items.object: Transformer inference infrastructure
items.answer: The thing that gets worse about inference than training is you lose a lot of the parallelism in the Transformer. Naively using a Transformer, you end up memory-bound, looking at your attention keys and values for every token you're generating. There's a lot of great work to do in both attacking this from a model-architecture perspective and from a hardware perspective, frankly, to get ourselves closer to the point where we're taking the massive computational power we have and making ourselves able to fully apply that to inference.
